title: A · One batch, end to end
why: Before any screen is drawn, somebody has to be able to describe a batch from the laboratory’s side as a sequence of things that happen and take time. This section is that description.
items: Walk one batch from start to finish from the laboratory’s side. What is the first thing you do, and the last?
How many times does the laboratory get involved in one batch? Roughly, not exactly.
Across the whole batch, how many hours of laboratory work is that in total?
Which of those involvements is the longest, and how long?
Which one is the most likely to make production wait?
Is the pattern the same for every batch, or does it change with the season or the raw material?
How many days of the 20 does the laboratory touch the batch at all? Which days are quiet?
Is there a day where the laboratory is doing several things for the same batch at once?
What does a normal day look like when two batches are running?
Is any part of the batch handled by someone other than the laboratory — production taking its own reading, for example?
What does the laboratory do for a batch that nobody has asked for, but that is done anyway?
What part of the batch does the laboratory feel it has no visibility of?

title: B · How long each test takes
why: The single most useful set of numbers in this whole document. Every scheduling decision the system makes depends on knowing how long a test takes — and "a test" means from sample in hand to a number that exists.
items: Moisture: how long from sample in hand to a number, start to finish?
C:N — is it calculated from the above, or is it its own test with its own time?
The visual checks — smell, colour, squeeze, actinomycetes: how long, together?
Heights — bunker, tunnel, shrunken: how long, and is it the laboratory that measures them or production?
For each of the above: how much of that time is the machine working, and how much is a person working?
Which of these can be left running unattended while something else is done?
Which of these needs the technician to stand there for the whole time?
If all the tests at one checkpoint are done together, is the total the sum of the parts, or less?
Is the time different for the first sample of the day versus the fifth?
Which test would you most like to be faster, and what makes it slow?

title: C · From sample to number — the gap that decides everything
why: The system needs to know not how long a test takes, but how long production waits. Those are different numbers and the difference is where the whole schedule lives.
items: For each checkpoint: how long between the sample being taken and production being told the answer?
Is that gap minutes, hours, or the next morning? Give the honest normal, not the best case.
Which checkpoints have a gap long enough that production has already moved on by the time the number exists?
Is production ever waiting, physically standing there, for a laboratory number? Which checkpoints?
When production is waiting, what is the longest it has actually waited?
Is the sample taken as soon as the material is ready, or at a fixed time?
How long can a sample sit before it is tested without the number changing?
Does the answer to that differ by test? Moisture especially.
Is the number ever given verbally before it is written down anywhere?
How much earlier could the laboratory be told a sample is coming, and would that help?
If the laboratory knew the whole day’s sampling schedule at 6am, what would change?
Which gap, if halved, would make the biggest difference to production?

title: D · Sequence and dependencies — what waits on what
why: This is the section that decides whether the system can schedule laboratory work at all, or only record it after the fact.
items: Which laboratory results must exist before production can move to the next step? Name them.
For each of those, what physically happens if the result is not there yet — does the material sit, or does work continue?
Is any laboratory test dependent on another test finishing first?
Does the laboratory ever hold a sample until a related sample arrives so both can be run together?
Is there a test that only makes sense if an earlier one came back a certain way?
Does an out-of-range result change what is tested next, or only what production does next?
Which laboratory work is time-critical — must happen within a window — and which can slide by a day?
For the ones with a window, how wide is the window?
What has to be prepared in advance — reagents, calibration, drying — and how long before?
Is anything tested that nothing downstream actually uses?

title: E · What runs at the same time
why: The process has real parallelism — paddy soaking alongside the main rail, six piles under two machines. The laboratory’s parallelism is what decides whether that is a problem.
items: Can the laboratory run more than one test at the same time? Which combinations?
Can two different batches be tested in the same session?
When six piles need the same test, are they done one after another or all together?
How much longer does six piles take than one pile? Six times, or less?
Is the paddy stream tested by the same person at the same bench as the main line?
Does testing the paddy soak ever collide with testing the main line? What gives way?
If two checkpoints fall due at the same hour, which one is done first, and who decides?
Is there a queue today, and how long does it get?
What is the most the laboratory has ever had waiting at once?

title: F · Equipment, and how many at once
why: Capacity is a hard ceiling the system cannot schedule around unless it knows where it is.
items: How many samples can the oven hold at once?
How many moisture meters are there, and how many people can use them at the same time?
How many pH and EC meters?
Is there one balance, or several?
Which piece of equipment is the bottleneck on a busy day?
How long does the oven take to be free again after a run?
Does anything need to cool, settle or stabilise before the next use, and for how long?
What happens when a meter is being calibrated — does testing stop?
How often does calibration happen, and how long does it take?
Is any test sent outside the factory? Which, and what is the turnaround in days?
If one more of any instrument were bought, which one, and how much time would it save?

title: G · People, shifts and cover
why: The system will ask somebody to do something at H317, which may be four in the morning. It needs to know whether anybody is there.
items: How many people work in the laboratory?
What hours does the laboratory actually work? Start and end.
Is there anybody in the laboratory at night?
What happens to a checkpoint that falls due at 2am?
Sundays and holidays — does the laboratory run?
Can any of these tests be done by a production operator rather than a technician? Which?
Who covers when the technician is on leave or sick?
Is there a handover between shifts, and what is passed on?
Does the same person do the sampling and the testing, or two people?
How long does it take a new person to be trusted with each test?
Is there work the laboratory does that is not testing at all — cleaning, preparation, paperwork — and how many hours a day?

title: H · The checkpoints, one at a time
why: For each of the 25, the system needs the same four numbers. Answer them as a row per checkpoint rather than as prose — a table is fine, a scribbled list is fine.
items: For each checkpoint: how long does the whole thing take, sample to number?
For each checkpoint: how many people are needed?
For each checkpoint: does production wait, or carry on?
For each checkpoint: how much warning does the laboratory need that it is coming?
Which of the 25 are done at a fixed time of day regardless of the batch?
Which of the 25 are done "when production calls"?
Are any of the 25 done together as one visit to the floor?
Are any of the 25 skipped in practice, and under what circumstances?
Are any of the 25 done more often than the process says?
Is there a checkpoint the laboratory does that is not in the list of 25?
Which of the 25 does the laboratory consider least useful?

title: I · The Turner window
why: Two readings, six piles, two machines, and a process that does not stop. This is the tightest timing in the whole batch and the one most likely to be got wrong in software.
items: Before T1 and after T1, six piles each — how long does the whole set of six take?
Is the "before T1" set taken all at once, or pile by pile as each pile is about to be turned?
How long before the T1 pass does the "before" sample need to be taken?
How soon after a pile is turned is the "after" sample taken?
Does the turner wait for the laboratory at any point, or never?
If the laboratory is not ready, does T1 go ahead without the reading?
Two machines turning at once — does that double the sampling load in the same hour?
Is the sample taken from the pile before the machine reaches it, or after it has passed?
Is a pile ever sampled twice because the first sample was taken at the wrong moment?
How long does the whole T1 pass take across six piles, from the laboratory’s point of view?
Would the laboratory want a reading at T0, T2 or T3 if it were free? What would it tell you?

title: J · Chicken manure and the 12-hour window
why: The one rule in the process that is already known to be conditional. The system needs to know exactly what the condition is measured between.
items: Under 12 hours between arrival and use means no re-test. Is 12 the right number?
Measured from arrival to what, exactly — unloading, mixing start, or something else?
How long does the arrival test itself take, from lorry to number?
Does the lorry wait for the arrival test, or is it unloaded first?
If the manure sits longer than the window, is the full set repeated or only part of it?
How often does manure actually sit longer than the window? Most loads, or rarely?
Does manure arrive in one load or several, and does each load get its own test?
How much notice does the laboratory get that manure is arriving?
Does covered versus uncovered storage change how fast it changes?
Has a load ever been rejected on arrival, and what happened to the batch that day?

title: K · When something goes wrong, and what it costs in time
why: Rework is a duration, and the system has to be able to plan for it. Every answer here should be a number of hours.
items: A result comes back out of range. What happens next, and how long does it take?
A retest — how long from deciding to retest to having the new number?
Moisture is low and misting is needed. How long is the misting, and how long before you re-measure?
After misting, is the re-measure the full test again, or a quicker check?
A sample is lost or spoiled. How long to get another one?
An instrument fails mid-batch. What happens, and how long is the delay?
Power fails during a drying run — is the result void, and how much time is lost?
How often does a checkpoint have to be repeated? Once a batch, once a month?
A batch is held longer than planned. Do any checkpoints have to be repeated, and which?
How long does the laboratory keep a sample in case it is needed again?
What is the longest a laboratory problem has ever delayed a batch?

title: L · Decisions the laboratory makes
why: Some readings are recorded. Some readings change what happens next. The system must know which is which, who decides, and how long the deciding takes.
items: Which laboratory readings actually change what production does next? Name them.
The moisture decision: at or above 68 proceed, below 67 mist. What happens between 67 and 68?
Who makes that call — the technician, the laboratory in charge, or production?
How long does that decision normally take once the number exists?
Does anyone have to approve a laboratory result before production acts on it?
If yes, who, and how long does that normally take?
At night and at weekends, who makes the call?
Is a decision ever made on a number before it is formally recorded?
Does production ever overrule the laboratory? What happens then?
How is the decision communicated — phone, in person, a book?
Is there a decision the laboratory would like to make but currently cannot?

title: M · What stops production, and for how long
why: Four checkpoints in the standard are marked as gates. This section checks whether they really are, and what happens on the floor when one bites.
items: Which laboratory results, if missing, actually stop production today?
When that happens, what does production do — wait, or continue and record it?
How long has production actually been stopped by the laboratory, at most?
Can anybody let production continue without the result? Who?
When that override happens, is anything written down?
Are there results the laboratory thinks should stop production but currently do not?
Are any of the four gates not really gates in practice?
Would a warning an hour before a gate is due be useful, or noise?
Should a result ever be too old to rely on? After how long?

title: N · How the number travels today
why: Understanding the current path from bench to decision is what tells us what the app has to replace, and what it must not break.
items: When a number exists, how does the person who needs it find out?
How long does that take — immediately, at the end of the shift, next morning?
Where is the number written down first?
Does the same number get written more than once, in more than one place?
Who else sees it, and when?
Is anything typed into a computer today? What, and by whom, and when?
At the end of a batch, is there a summary of all its laboratory results anywhere?
How long does producing that summary take?
Has a number ever gone missing between the bench and the person who needed it?

When an out-of-range number is reported, what happens to the person who reported it — nothing, a question, or a problem? Answer this one plainly; it predicts the quality of every number the system will collect.
What does management ask the laboratory for, and how long does answering take?

title: O · What makes a test take longer than usual
why: Averages are useless for scheduling if the variance is large. This section is about the spread, not the middle.
items: On a bad day, how much longer does a moisture result take than on a good day?
What is the usual cause of a delay — waiting for the sample, waiting for equipment, or waiting for a person?
Does the time of day change how long things take?
Does the weather change anything — humidity, rain, the material being wetter?
Is the first batch of a season slower than a settled one?
Does a new technician change these times, and by how much?
Which test has the most unpredictable duration?
If you had to promise production a time for each result, what would you promise?

title: P · Capacity — where the laboratory breaks
why: The factory intends to run more batches. The system should be able to say, in advance, when that stops being possible.
items: How many batches can run at once before the laboratory cannot keep up?
On the busiest day of a batch, how many hours of laboratory work is there?
Which day of the 20 is the busiest for the laboratory, and why?
If two batches were offset by a few days, would that help or make it worse?
What is the first thing that would be dropped if the laboratory ran out of time?
Is any of the current work done outside normal hours because there is no room in the day?
At what number of simultaneous batches does the laboratory need another person?
At what number does it need another instrument?

title: Q · What the laboratory is waiting on from everybody else
why: The laboratory is not only a source of delay; it is usually also a victim of one. The system can fix some of these for free.
items: What does the laboratory most often wait for that is not its own doing?
How much notice does the laboratory get before a sample is needed today?
How much notice would be enough?
Is the laboratory ever told about a batch after it has already started?
Does the laboratory know the plan for the next 24 hours? How?
When production changes the plan, how does the laboratory find out?
Is the laboratory ever asked for a test that was not planned, and how often?
What one piece of information, given earlier, would save the laboratory the most time?

title: R · Tomorrow — what the app has to do on day one
why: These are the only questions that must be answered before the APK is built. Everything above can be answered during the first batch; these cannot.
items: What is the batch identifier for tomorrow’s batch? The exact text, as it will be said out loud.
What stage will that batch be at when the app is handed over?
Which checkpoints will realistically be hit in the first 48 hours?
How many phones, and who gets which — laboratory, operator, supervisor?
Who trains them, and how long does that take?
Is there signal where the samples are taken and where the tests are done?
Will they also keep the paper record tomorrow, in parallel? (They should.)
If the app is wrong or confusing tomorrow, who do they call?
If the app fails entirely, does work stop or continue on paper?
What single thing, at the end of tomorrow, would make you call it a success?
